KANJIDON / NEXT STOP: TOKYO

Tokyo trains and subway: 10 tips to enjoy the ride.

First time in Tokyo? Let's start with the basics: paying for rides, finding the right train and leaving the station near your hotel. Then we'll fit in a ride with a bay view, too.

Kanjidon Team · Research updated September 25, 2026

A HUGE CITY. ONE SMALL TIP.Start with where you want to go. One stop at a time.
The linesSuicaPasses and pricesWhere to stayThe kanji challenge

Your first Tokyo subway map looks like a very ambitious plate of spaghetti. Then you take your first ride, hear the gate go beep, and something lovely happens: it starts to make sense.

You don't need to learn the whole map. Open a maps app, enter your destination and choose public transport. It will show you which lines to take and where to change. Let's make those directions, tickets and first journeys feel easy.

01 / LET'S MEET THE TEAM

You'll take the subway.
And a few city trains, too.

Getting around Tokyo usually means using both the subway and trains that connect its neighborhoods. Tokyo Metro and Toei are the two subway operators. JR East is a railway company: it runs the Yamanote, a train line that loops through many well-known neighborhoods. All are useful for exploring, even though different companies run them.

Tokyo Metro + ToeiThey run the subway lines.
JR EastIt runs city trains, including the Yamanote.
Other companiesThey run other lines, including routes to the bay and airports.

One handy way to pay is Suica: a card you load with money, with each fare taken from its balance. It works on the subway and many city trains, including the Yamanote. PASMO is another card of this kind. Here's how they work.

THE TIP TO TAKE WITH YOU

You don't need to memorize the companies. Follow the line name shown in your app. The distinction matters when buying a pass: some cover only the subway, so you can't use them on the Yamanote.

02 / THE MOST SATISFYING BEEP OF YOUR TRIP

What's a Suica?
A little wallet for your journeys.

“IC card” is the term used for these rechargeable electronic cards. Suica and PASMO are two examples. Put money on one and use it to pay, without buying a new ticket for every ride. They aren't unlimited-travel passes.

Here's what to do:
1. Load some money onto your card.
2. Tap it on the reader at the ticket gate to enter the station.
3. Tap again when you leave at your destination: the system calculates the fare and deducts it from your balance.
Use the same card to enter and leave. Each traveler needs their own.

Use a physical card or a digital version if your phone supports it. For a physical card, keep some yen in cash for the compatible top-up machines in stations. For a phone version, check device and payment-card compatibility before traveling. Not enough balance to leave? Use a fare-adjustment machine or ask the staff by the gates.

03 / COLOR IS JUST THE START

Look for the letter, number
and direction.

Each subway line has a color and letter; each station has a number too. Ginza is the yellow line marked G. Going from Ueno to Asakusa, two popular sightseeing areas? Ueno is G16, Asakusa is G19. Follow the Ginza signs toward Asakusa. Three stops and you're there.

G16Ueno→G17Inaricho→G18Tawaramachi→G19Asakusa

Color helps you find the line. Direction puts you on the right platform. And the number gives you that little “got it” moment before you've even learned to read the names.

04 / YOUR NEW FAVORITE LINE

Use the Yamanote.
But check the shortcuts, too.

The Yamanote is a train line linking some of Tokyo's best-known neighborhoods, including Shibuya, Shinjuku and Ueno. It gets you close to lots of places you'll want to visit, so you'll probably get to know it quite well. Imagine a big loop around the city, with trains running in both directions.

On the platform, look for the major neighborhoods listed next on the signs. At Shinjuku, for example, one direction heads toward Shibuya and Shinagawa, the other toward Ikebukuro and Ueno.

THE TIP THAT CUTS ACROSS THE LOOP

Heading from Shinjuku to Tokyo Station? Check the Chūō Rapid, another JR train line. It crosses the city instead of following the Yamanote loop. Your maps app can help you choose the quickest route for your departure time.

Lines and directions from Shinjuku, JR East ↗

A RIDE WITH A VIEW: THE YURIKAMOME

The Yurikamome is an automatic, driverless train on an elevated track, above street level. It connects Shimbashi and Toyosu via Odaiba, on Tokyo Bay, and crosses the Rainbow Bridge. The journey itself is part of the sightseeing.

If there's room at the front, enjoy the view through the front window: for a moment, it feels like you're driving. You can pay with Suica or PASMO, but the Tokyo Subway Ticket doesn't cover the Yurikamome. And those similar names? Yamanote and Yurikamome are two different lines!

Yurikamome route and highlights ↗

05 / YOUR PASS SHOULD FOLLOW YOUR PLANS

Pay for each ride or get a pass?
It depends on how much you travel.

With Suica, each ride comes out of the money you loaded onto your card. A pass lets you ride as often as you like for a set period, but only on the lines it covers. Choose your sightseeing plans first, then compare costs. For your first outing, using Suica is perfectly fine. You don't have to find the perfect pass before you can start exploring.

Subway pass prices checked September 25, 2026. Confirm conditions, format and prices on official pages before buying.

24 HOURS REALLY MEANS 24 HOURS

The Tokyo Subway Ticket clock starts with your first use: start at 3 pm and the 24-hour version lasts until 3 pm the next day. For digital tickets, also follow the activation instructions for the format you buy.

YOU STAY ON THE TRAIN, BUT THE COMPANY CHANGES

Sometimes the same train continues onto a line run by another company. You stay in your seat, but your pass might not cover that part of the journey: you pay separately for the extra section. For airport trips, always check what your ticket includes.

Here's an example: if your subway journeys over 24 hours would cost 1,200 yen in total, the 1,000-yen pass saves you 200 yen. If they cost 800 yen, paying with Suica is cheaper. Only count journeys covered by the pass when comparing.

06 / THE REAL TREASURE IS THE EXIT

Check where you're going.
Then choose the nearest exit.

“I'll get off at Shinjuku” is a start. “I'll leave on my hotel's side” is a plan. In big stations, choosing your exit before heading above ground can save you a long walk with your suitcase.

Exits have numbers or labels such as “3” or “A8”. Follow those signs to reach the right side of the street. Check which exit your hotel or maps app recommends. With a suitcase or stroller, look for the elevator symbol too: the nearest exit isn't always the easiest.

YOUR TINY DON'T-GET-LOST KIT

A screenshot of the route, your hotel's name in Japanese and the exit to look for. Three tiny things that beat ten open browser tabs.

07 / YOUR HOLIDAY STARTS AT THE STATION NEAR YOUR HOTEL

Stay close to the tracks.
Your feet are already thanking you.

Look for a hotel about five minutes' walk from a station that works for the places you want to visit. Before booking, look up the journey from the hotel to two or three of your planned stops in your maps app: you'll soon get a feel for it. Check which exit you'll use too, because the biggest stations cover a lot of ground.

These three are strong contenders for convenient transport links, with access checked on the hotels' own websites. Your final choice depends on budget, rooms and the neighborhood you want to enjoy.

UENO / FIRST TIME IN TOKYO

NOHGA Hotel
Ueno Tokyo

For mixing parks, museums and city adventures.

3 minutes from Ueno subway station (Ginza and Hibiya); about 5 minutes from JR Ueno. For the subway, the hotel lists Exit 3 and an elevator route between Exits 2 and 3.

SHIBUYA / RIGHT IN THE ACTION

Shibuya
Stream Hotel

For stepping straight into Shibuya's rhythm.

Connected to Exit C2 at Shibuya Station and the new south entrance for JR trains. You can catch both the subway and other trains here. Follow the signs for your line: the platforms are on different levels.

SHIBA / A QUIETER RETURN

The Celestine
Tokyo Shiba

For a base in the Shiba area with several stations to choose from.

1 minute from Exit A2 at Shibakoen Station, but there are stairs. With a suitcase, the hotel recommends Mita Station: Exit A8 has an elevator and is about 3 minutes away. JR Tamachi Station is about a 7-minute walk away.

Walking times are supplied by the hotels, not measured from the platform or train door. Availability and prices depend on your dates.

08 / COFFEE CAN BE A STRATEGY

Let the rush pass.
Then ride with more room.

If you can, avoid the busiest weekday periods: roughly 7:30 to 9:30 am and 5:30 to 7:30 pm. A lovely excuse for a slow breakfast or one last neighborhood stroll.

On the platform, follow the marked queues, let people off before boarding and keep your backpack in front or out of other people's way. Phone on silent, calls for later: there's a whole city to watch through the window.

Times and travel manners, GO TOKYO ↗

09 / ONE MORE STOP, ONE EYE ON THE CLOCK

Check your way back.
Then enjoy the evening.

Tokyo's subway and trains stop running overnight. Many last departures are around midnight, but the time depends on your route. It's worth checking yours before heading out for dinner.

Look up the whole journey back to your hotel and select the last-departure option if available. If you need to change trains, you must catch the second one too. Making it onto the first isn't enough.

BONUS: SOMETIMES WALKING WINS

For two nearby places, compare the walking time too. Once you count stairs, corridors, waiting and the way back up, a single stop can lose to ten minutes exploring a new little street.

10 / NEXT STOP: “I CAN READ THAT!”

Turn the signs
into a little kanji treasure hunt.

Kanji are characters used in Japanese writing, including station names. The names also appear in Latin letters, so you can find your way without knowing Japanese. But recognizing 東京 before reading “Tokyo” underneath? That satisfaction is all yours.

Start with a few names you'll actually encounter. Notice the characters, connect them to the sound and spot them again the next day. The city becomes one giant review session, with far more snack breaks.

東京Tōkyō

東 = east
京 = capital

新宿Shinjuku

新 = new
宿 = lodging

上野Ueno

上 = above
野 = field, plain

These meanings help you remember the individual characters. To pronounce a station name, learn the whole word: Tokyo, Shinjuku, Ueno.

Tiny challenge: which character appears again in Kyoto?

京都 is read Kyōto. You've found 京, the same character as in 東京. A familiar piece in a new name. That's where the fun begins.

PACK A FEW KANJI FOR TOKYO, TOO

The next station?
You might read it yourself.

Download Kanjidon and start practicing kanji, meanings and readings with cards, quizzes and review. It's a fun way to get your eyes ready for what you'll encounter in Japan.

The English on the signs is still wonderfully handy. That little “hey, I know this one” is wonderfully yours.

Suica in your pocket. A few kanji in your head. Off you go.
